newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Shell, Agip in Romania LPG project.
newsitem.headline: Shell, Agip in Romania LPG project.

text.p: The Romanian units of Royal Dutch/Shell Group and Agip SpA of Italy said on Wednesday they had joined forces to develop new markets for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

The Romanian Association of Liquefied Gas (ARGPL) has been formed to ensure that the latest technology is used in local LPG activities, Angela Ugon, marketing manager of Shell Gas Romania, told a news conference.
ButanGas Romania, a joint venture between Italy's Butan Gas SpA and Romania's Competrol SA oil products retailer is also a founding member of the ARGPL.
Ugon said ARGPL's immediate plans focused on developing markets for fixed LPG bulk tanks, which are new in Romania.

The Association would also work closely with local equipment makers in Romania to ensure that the equipment for filling plants, transportation, bulk tanks and appliances are made to international standards, she said.
The local media has reported many accidents from explosions of defective locally-made gas bottles.
Ugon cited hotels, farming and the automotive industry as among the potential clients for LPG.
Romania's annual average LPG demand is some 450,000 tonnes. Estimates say this could rise to 600,000 tonnes by the year 2000.
But in the past years local refineries have only been able to supply around 300,000 tonnes a year, due to cuts in imports of crude oil, from which the LPG is processed.

An acute shortage of hard currency has forced Romania to drastically cut its crude imports this year. Long lines of people queuing with gas bottles at filling stations across the country have been a common sight over the past months.

Anthony Nicholson, general manager of Shell Gas Romania, said his company has had to import some 5,000 tonnes of LPG and has ordered another 3,000 tonnes to overcome problems created by the LPG shortages at local refineries.
He said a planned LPG terminal in the Black Sea port of Constanta was vital to boost the industry.
"The terminal in Constanta is essential for the future development of the LPG business in Romania and it may also be beneficial for Hungary as well," Nicholson said.
But the project, which requires an estimated $100 million to complete, has not yet gone beyond feasability studies and no implementation timetable has been announced.

Nicholson said alternatives being considered included importing LPG from Russia to be delivered at railway transfer points or from small tankers and barges on the river Danube. -- Adrian Dascalu, Bucharest Newsroom +40 1 3120264
